content: Dexlansoprazole can cause severe skin reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN). These conditions can result in painful red or purple skin that appears burned and peels off, flat red rashes or blisters on the skin, mouth, nose, and genitals, and red, painful, watery eyes. If you experience any of these symptoms, stop taking the medication immediately and seek emergency medical attention. Dexlansoprazole may also cause a serious allergic reaction known as DRESS (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms), which can affect multiple organs, including the liver, kidneys, and heart. Symptoms of DRESS include skin rash or hives, fever, swollen lymph nodes, shortness of breath, swelling in the feet, ankles, or legs, dark-colored urine, and yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice). If you notice any of these symptoms, discontinue the medication and contact your healthcare provider immediately. This medication can exacerbate or induce lupus, an autoimmune disorder where the immune system attacks the body’s own tissues. Symptoms of lupus include new or worsening joint pain and rashes on the arms or cheeks. Notify your healthcare provider if you experience these symptoms. Long-term use of dexlansoprazole (three years or more) can lead to vitamin B-12 deficiency, as it reduces the absorption of this vitamin. Symptoms of deficiency include a sore tongue, weakness, and tingling or numbness in the hands or feet. If you experience these symptoms, stop the medication and consult your healthcare provider. Dexlansoprazole can also cause hypomagnesemia, a condition characterized by low magnesium levels in the blood. This can lead to seizures, abnormal heart rhythms, dizziness, muscle spasms, or changes in heart rate. Individuals taking the medication for extended periods or in combination with other drugs that lower magnesium levels are at higher risk. If you experience any of these symptoms, stop the medication and contact your healthcare provider. Prolonged use of dexlansoprazole, especially in older adults or at high doses, may increase the risk of bone loss and fractures. Discuss this risk with your healthcare provider if you are concerned. Severe allergic reactions to dexlansoprazole can occur, presenting as breathing difficulties, wheezing, a racing heart, fever, swollen lymph nodes, swelling of the face, lips, mouth, tongue, or throat, trouble swallowing, itching, hives, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, or stomach cramps. If you experience any of these symptoms, stop the medication and seek immediate medical attention. Dexlansoprazole should not be used by individuals allergic to its ingredients, other proton pump inhibitors, or specific components of the product. Consult your pharmacist for a complete list of ingredients. This medication may interact with other drugs, such as methotrexate, digoxin, warfarin, tacrolimus, certain antiretroviral medications, St. John’s Wort, and rifampin. Always inform your healthcare provider about all prescription and over-the-counter medications, supplements, and herbal products you are taking to avoid potential interactions. Dexlansoprazole is not recommended for immediate relief of heartburn, as it may take 1 to 4 days to take full effect. It should only be used as prescribed by a healthcare provider and not shared with others, even if they have similar symptoms. Store dexlansoprazole at room temperature (68°F to 77°F or 20°C to 25°C) and keep it out of reach of children. Do not chew, cut, or crush the capsules. If swallowing is difficult, the capsule contents can be sprinkled on a tablespoon of applesauce and consumed immediately without mixing with other foods. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take double doses. Dexlansoprazole is used to treat conditions caused by excess stomach acid, such as gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and erosive esophagitis (EE). It works by reducing the amount of acid produced in the stomach. If you suspect an overdose, seek medical help immediately by calling 911 or contacting a Poison Control Center at 800-222-1222.
